rw: There are 3 red marbles out of 3 + 7 = 10 total, so the probability of drawing red is 3/10, which equals 0.3.

ww.3: A probability can never exceed 1, so 3 is impossible; the correct fraction is 3 red out of 10 marbles, which is 0.3.
ww.0.37: The value 0.37 does not match any ratio here, because 3 red out of 10 marbles gives exactly 3/10 = 0.3, not 0.37.
ww.0.7: The value 0.7 is the probability of drawing blue, since 7 of the 10 marbles are blue, but the question asks about red marbles.

rw: A fair six-sided die has six equally likely faces and only one of them shows a 5, so the probability is 1 out of 6.

ww.1/5: The value 1/5 would apply to a five-sided die, but a fair six-sided die has six equally likely faces, so one face gives 1/6.
ww.5/6: The fraction 5/6 is the chance of rolling anything except a 5, which is the complement; the chance of rolling a 5 itself is 1/6.
ww.1/2: The fraction 1/2 would mean three of the six faces show a 5, but only one face does, so the correct probability is 1/6.

rw: The even faces are 2, 4 and 6, which is 3 of the 6 equally likely faces, so the probability is 3/6, which simplifies to 1/2.

ww.1/6: The fraction 1/6 is the chance of one single face, but an even roll can be 2, 4 or 6, which is three faces, not one.
ww.2/3: The fraction 2/3 would need four even faces, but a die has only three even faces: 2, 4 and 6, giving 3/6 = 1/2.
ww.1/3: The fraction 1/3 would mean only two faces are even, but 2, 4 and 6 are all even, so there are three, giving 3/6 = 1/2.

rw: Independent events have outcomes that do not change each other's probabilities, so P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B), as with two separate coin flips.

ww.They cannot both happen at the same mome: Events that cannot both happen at once are mutually exclusive, not independent; independence is about one outcome not changing the probability of the other.
ww.They are the same event described in two: Two independent events are different events, not one event described twice; they just do not influence each other's probabilities, so describing them as identical is wrong.
ww.They always happen together, so one neve: Events that always occur together are strongly dependent, since one outcome determines the other; independence means knowing one result tells you nothing about the other's chance.

rw: The flips are independent, so multiply the chances: 1/2 times 1/2 = 1/4, meaning one of four equally likely outcomes (HH, HT, TH, TT) is two heads.

ww.1: A probability of 1 would mean two heads is certain, but each flip has only a 1/2 chance, so the combined chance is 1/4.
ww.2: A probability cannot be greater than 1, so 2 is impossible; two heads in a row has chance 1/2 times 1/2 = 1/4.
ww.1/2: The value 1/2 is the chance of heads on a single flip; for two consecutive heads you multiply 1/2 times 1/2 to get 1/4.

rw: The two rolls are independent, so multiply the chances: 1/6 times 1/6 = 1/36, which matches 1 favorable outcome out of 36 possible pairs.

ww.2/6: The fraction 2/6 adds the single-roll chances (1/6 + 1/6), but independent events must be multiplied, so the answer is 1/6 times 1/6 = 1/36.
ww.1/6: The value 1/6 is the chance of one 6 on a single roll; getting a second 6 as well multiplies by another 1/6, giving 1/36.
ww.1/12: The value 1/12 would come from 1/6 times 1/2, but the second roll also has a 1/6 chance of a 6, so the product is 1/36.

rw: Mutually exclusive events cannot both occur in one trial, such as rolling a 2 and a 5 on one die, so their joint probability is zero.

ww.Independent events that never affect oth: Independent events can happen together while not affecting each other, so that describes independence, whereas mutually exclusive events are those that cannot happen at the same time.
ww.Events that always happen at the same mo: Events that always happen at the same moment are the opposite of mutually exclusive; mutually exclusive events never happen together in a single trial.
ww.Equally likely events in a single trial: Equally likely events share the same probability, which is a different idea from mutual exclusivity; two equally likely events could still happen together, like heads on two coins.

rw: The complement of an event is every outcome in the sample space where the event does not occur, and its probability equals 1 minus P(event).

ww.The event itself as it occurs in the sam: The event itself is the set of outcomes where it occurs, which is the opposite of its complement, since the complement contains the outcomes outside the event.
ww.A guess about the chance of the event in: A guess about the chance is only an estimate and not an outcome set; the complement is a defined set of outcomes in which the event fails.
ww.A different event that cannot happen wit: An event that cannot occur with the first is mutually exclusive but need not cover everything else; the complement must include every remaining outcome, so exclusivity alone is not enough.

rw: The chance of no rain is the complement of rain, so subtract from 1: 1 - 0.35 = 0.65, meaning a 65 percent chance of staying dry.

ww.1.35: Probabilities cannot exceed 1, so 1.35 is impossible; the chance of no rain is 1 minus 0.35, which gives 0.65.
ww.0.35: The value 0.35 is the chance of rain itself, not of its absence; the complement is 1 - 0.35 = 0.65.
ww.0.35%: The value 0.35% means 0.0035, which is far too small; the correct answer is 1 - 0.35 = 0.65, not a tiny percentage.

rw: The law of large numbers says that as more observations are collected, the sample average gets closer to the true expected value, so large samples are more reliable.

ww.Outliers dominate large samples, so the: Large samples do the opposite of letting outliers dominate, because any single odd value is diluted by many others and the average moves toward the true value.
ww.Small samples are best because they are: Small samples are less reliable because chance can swing their averages widely; the law of large numbers says bigger samples converge on the true mean.
ww.Averages never converge toward any value: Averages do converge toward a value as more data are gathered, which is precisely what the law of large numbers states, so claiming they never converge is false.

rw: Expected value is the sum of each outcome times its probability, which gives the average result you would see over many repeated trials in the long run.

ww.A guaranteed value that the outcome will: Expected value is an average over many trials, not a guarantee; a single trial can land far from it, as a fair coin never pays half a head.
ww.The most likely value that a single tria: Expected value is not the most likely outcome of one trial; it is a probability-weighted average and may be a value that never actually occurs.
ww.The largest value that a single trial co: Expected value is not the maximum possible result; it sits among the possible values, weighting each outcome by its probability, so it is usually below the largest outcome.

rw: Multiply each payout by its probability and add: 10 times 0.2 plus 0 times 0.8 = 2 + 0 = $2, which is the long-run average per game.

ww.$8: The value $8 is wrong because it ignores the probabilities; the expected value is 10 times 0.2 plus 0 times 0.8, which equals $2.
ww.$0.2: The value $0.2 is the probability of winning, not a dollar amount; the expected value multiplies it by the $10 payout, giving 10 times 0.2 = $2.
ww.$10: The value $10 is the prize when winning, but you win only 20 percent of the time, so the average is 10 times 0.2 = $2.

rw: A correlation of -0.9 is close to -1, meaning that as one variable rises the other tends to fall strongly, which is a strong negative relationship.

ww.A perfect positive relationship: A perfect positive relationship would have a correlation of +1; the negative sign on -0.9 means the variables move in opposite directions.
ww.No relationship at all there: No relationship would give a correlation near 0; a value of -0.9 is far from zero, so a strong linear pattern is present.
ww.A weak positive relationship: A weak positive relationship would show a small positive value such as +0.2; -0.9 is both negative and large in size, so it is strong.

rw: A correlation near 0 means the points do not follow a straight-line trend, so there is little or no linear relationship between the variables.

ww.A strong positive linear link: A strong positive linear link would have a correlation close to +1; a value near 0 means there is no such pattern in the data.
ww.A strong negative linear link: A strong negative linear link would have a correlation close to -1; a value near 0 is nowhere near that, so no such pattern exists.
ww.A perfect linear relationship: A perfect linear relationship gives a correlation of exactly +1 or -1; a value near 0 is the opposite extreme, showing almost no linear link.

rw: Two variables can move together because a hidden third factor drives both, or by chance, so a correlation alone cannot show that one causes the other.

ww.Correlation always proves cause, as vari: Correlation never proves cause, because two variables can move together due to a shared third factor or coincidence, so a link in the data alone does not show causation.
ww.Causation is impossible to ever show in: Causation can be shown with well-designed experiments, such as randomized trials, so it is not impossible; the point is that correlation alone cannot establish it.
ww.Correlation is random, so it has no link: Correlation is a real measured pattern and not random noise, but a pattern can arise from other factors, which is why it does not by itself imply cause.

rw: Hot summer weather drives more swimming, which raises drownings, and also raises ice cream buying, so weather is a confounding variable behind both patterns.

ww.Drowning causes ice cream sales: Drowning does not cause ice cream sales; both numbers rise in summer, so the link is not one causing the other, and the hidden factor is the weather.
ww.Pure coincidence only, nothing more: The rise in both is not pure coincidence, because a real shared cause exists in hot weather, which brings more swimmers and more ice cream buyers at once.
ww.Ice cream causes drowning deaths: Eating ice cream does not cause drowning; the two simply rise together because warm summer weather increases both swimming and ice cream purchases, so this is a spurious link.

rw: A confounding variable is an outside factor that affects both the supposed cause and the effect, which can create a false link or mask a real one.

ww.The outcome that a researcher measures a: The outcome measured at the end of an experiment is the dependent variable, not a confounder; a confounder is a separate outside factor that influences both cause and effect.
ww.The only variable in a study, which the: The variable the researcher changes on purpose is the independent variable; a confounder is not controlled by the researcher and instead distorts the apparent relationship between variables.
ww.The sample of people who are chosen to t: The group chosen to take part is the sample; a confounding variable is not a group of people but a hidden factor that influences both cause and effect.

rw: A hypothesis test is a procedure that weighs sample evidence to decide whether a claim about a population is supported or should be rejected.

ww.A way to collect data from a sample of p: Collecting data from a sample with a survey is data collection, not testing; a hypothesis test is the step that uses that sample data to judge a claim.
ww.A chart that shows the results of a test: A chart displays results but does not decide anything; a hypothesis test is a statistical procedure that uses sample data to judge whether a claim about a population holds.
ww.A database query that pulls a set of rec: A database query retrieves stored records and has nothing to do with statistics; a hypothesis test checks whether sample data support a claim about a population.

rw: The null hypothesis is the default assumption of no effect or no difference, and a test asks whether the data give enough evidence to reject it.

ww.A proven fact the data have already conf: The null is not a proven fact; it is only a starting assumption, and a test can reject it but never prove it true.
ww.A claim of a big effect, hoped to be pro: A claim of a big effect that the researcher hopes to prove is the alternative hypothesis, which is the opposite of the null's claim of no effect.
ww.A sample statistic such as the mean of t: A sample statistic such as the mean describes the data you collected, whereas the null hypothesis is a claim about the population that the statistic is used to test.

rw: Because p = 0.02 is smaller than the significance level of 0.05, the result is statistically significant, so we reject the null hypothesis.

ww.The result is impossible: A p-value of 0.02 does not make the result impossible; it only means the data would be fairly unlikely if the null were true, so the null is rejected.
ww.Collect no more data at all: A small p-value is a result to act on, not a reason to stop; we conclude from this test, and more data is not required.
ww.Accept the null as proven: Hypothesis tests never prove the null; since p = 0.02 is below 0.05 the data actually argue against the null, so it is rejected instead.

rw: A margin of error states how far a survey estimate may plausibly differ from the true population value, giving a range of uncertainty around the estimate, such as plus or minus 3 points.

ww.The mean of the sample data collected in: The mean of the sample is the estimate itself, not its uncertainty; the margin of error is the range around that estimate within which the true value likely falls.
ww.The sample size, which is the number of: The number of people asked is the sample size, which affects the margin of error but is not the same thing; the margin is the range of uncertainty.
ww.A data entry mistake made by a clerk at: A data entry mistake is a recording error, while the margin of error is a statistical measure of sampling uncertainty that exists even when all the data are recorded correctly.

rw: A result is statistically significant when it would be unlikely to appear through random chance alone, typically when the p-value falls below a chosen level such as 0.05.

ww.The data are clean and free of errors in: Clean data free of errors is about data quality, not significance; statistical significance means a result is unlikely to be explained by random chance alone.
ww.The sample is large enough to include ev: A sample large enough to include everyone would be a census, not significance; significance describes whether an observed result is unlikely to be due to chance.
ww.The effect is important in practice, as: Practical importance is about the size of the effect, while statistical significance only says the result is unlikely to be chance; a tiny effect can be significant in a large sample.

rw: A Type I error is a false positive: the null hypothesis is actually true, yet the test rejects it, and its probability is the significance level alpha.

ww.Failing to reject a false null hypothesi: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis is a Type II error, a false negative, whereas a Type I error is rejecting a null that is actually true.
ww.A correct decision made by the analyst a: A correct decision is not an error at all; a Type I error occurs only when the analyst wrongly rejects a null hypothesis that is true.
ww.A data entry mistake made by a clerk at: A data entry mistake is a recording problem, not a statistical decision error; a Type I error specifically means rejecting a true null hypothesis.

rw: A Type II error is a false negative: the null hypothesis is false, yet the test fails to reject it, so a real effect goes undetected.

ww.Rejecting a true null hypothesis, a fals: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is a Type I error, a false positive; a Type II error is the opposite mistake of missing a real effect.
ww.A correct decision made by the analyst a: A correct decision is not an error; a Type II error occurs when the test fails to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false.
ww.A data entry mistake made by a clerk whe: A data entry mistake is a clerical slip and not a hypothesis testing result; a Type II error means failing to reject a false null.

rw: Common methods are dropping records with gaps or imputing estimates such as the mean or median, which keep the dataset usable while limiting bias from the missing values.

ww.Ignoring them always and never filling i: Ignoring missing values always is not a valid rule, since gaps can bias results or break calculations; analysts usually remove records or fill the gaps with sensible estimates.
ww.Replacing the gaps with random text take: Random text from another column would corrupt the data and mix up meanings; missing numeric values should be filled with sensible estimates such as the mean or median instead.
ww.Deleting the entire dataset whenever any: Deleting the entire dataset because one value is missing would waste all other useful information; analysts remove only affected records or fill gaps with estimates.

rw: Normalization rescales features onto a common range or scale, such as 0 to 1, so that no feature dominates just because its numbers are larger.

ww.Making data normal in distribution only: Normalization or scaling is not about making data bell-shaped; it adjusts values to a common scale so that features can be compared fairly, and distribution shape may stay unchanged.
ww.Deleting outliers from the data and keep: Removing outliers is a cleaning step, whereas normalization keeps all values and only rescales them to a common scale so features are comparable.
ww.Encrypting data so that only approved us: Encrypting data is a security task; normalization is a scaling step that puts features on a similar range and does nothing to protect data from readers.

rw: One-hot encoding turns a categorical variable into binary columns, one per category, with a 1 marking the category present, so models can use it as numbers.

ww.Encrypting data so that only approved us: Encryption protects data from unauthorized readers; one-hot encoding is a format change that turns categories into binary columns and offers no security at all.
ww.Scaling numbers so that all of them fall: Scaling to a 0 to 1 range is normalization or min-max scaling, which is a different task; one-hot encoding creates a binary column for each category.
ww.Deleting categories that appear rarely i: Deleting or merging rare categories is a grouping step; one-hot encoding keeps every category and gives each its own binary column.

rw: A scatter plot puts one numeric variable on each axis, so each point shows a pair and the pattern reveals how the two variables relate.

ww.Bar chart: A bar chart compares values across categories using one numeric measure, so it does not show how two numeric variables move together.
ww.Word cloud: A word cloud displays the frequency of words in text, not numeric variables, so it cannot show a relationship between two numerical quantities.
ww.Pie chart: A pie chart shows parts of one whole as slices and uses a single measure, so it cannot display how two numeric variables relate.

rw: A line chart connects points in time order, so rises and falls across days, months or years are easy to see, which suits change over time.

ww.Pie chart: A pie chart shows how a whole splits into parts at one moment, so it cannot display how a value changes across time.
ww.Table of names: A table of names lists labels with no values plotted over time, so it cannot show trends or changes, and names alone carry no time pattern.
ww.Scatter plot: A scatter plot shows the relationship between two numeric variables, not a sequence of changes through time, though it could plot time on an axis; a line chart is the standard choice.

rw: A pie chart splits a circle into slices sized by share, so it shows how parts make up a whole, such as budget categories adding to 100 percent.

ww.Histogram: A histogram shows how values are distributed in bins for one numeric variable, not how parts add up to a whole.
ww.Line chart: A line chart tracks how a value changes over time, so it does not display parts that make up a whole.
ww.Scatter plot: A scatter plot shows the relationship between two numeric variables, not how shares combine to form a whole.

rw: A bar chart gives each category its own bar, so heights are easy to compare directly across categories such as products or regions.

ww.Line chart: A line chart is best for trends across time, not for comparing separate categories side by side.
ww.Scatter plot: A scatter plot shows how two numeric variables relate, not how a measure compares across separate categories.
ww.Heat map: A heat map uses color intensity across a grid, which suits dense matrices or patterns, whereas a bar chart makes direct comparisons across categories simpler and clearer.

rw: A heat map uses color intensity to represent values, so high and low areas stand out at a glance, whether in a grid or on a map.

ww.A text report that lists numbers in rows: A text report listing numbers in rows and columns is a table, whereas a heat map turns values into colors so patterns stand out visually.
ww.A list of names and addresses kept in a: A list of names and addresses is a contact record, not a visual; a heat map shades cells or areas by value to show intensity.
ww.A weather forecast only, with the temper: Heat maps are not limited to weather; they are used for website clicks, correlations and many other data, so restricting them to temperatures is wrong.

rw: Starting the axis above zero makes small differences look big because bar lengths no longer reflect true proportions, so truncating exaggerates differences between bars.

ww.It has no effect on the way bars look: Truncating the axis changes how long each bar appears, so it does affect how bars look; bar length should reflect the true size starting from zero.
ww.It improves the accuracy of the chart: Truncation does not improve accuracy; it distorts the proportions between bars, making small gaps look large and misleading the reader.
ww.It hides all differences between the bar: A truncated axis does the opposite of hiding differences; by cutting off the lower part of the scale it makes differences look bigger than they are.

rw: KPI stands for key performance indicator, a measurable value such as monthly sales that shows how well progress is going toward a goal.

ww.A kind of chart used to show key figures: A chart is a visual display, whereas a KPI is a measurable number tracked against a goal; a KPI can appear on a chart but is not itself one.
ww.A database key used to link one table to: A database key links tables, which is a database concept, while a KPI is a measurable value that shows progress toward a business goal.
ww.A keyboard shortcut that lets a user per: A keyboard shortcut triggers an action by key presses, which is a computing convenience, whereas a KPI is a metric used to track performance against objectives.

rw: Data storytelling blends data, visuals and narrative to explain insights clearly, so that the audience understands them and is moved to take action.

ww.Hiding data so that nobody can see the n: Hiding data means nobody sees the numbers, the opposite of storytelling, which exposes the data and explains what it means so people understand it.
ww.Deleting data that does not support the: Deleting data that does not support a story is cherry-picking and is dishonest, whereas data storytelling presents the real evidence clearly and honestly.
ww.Writing fiction that tells an invented t: Writing fiction about an invented company has no real data behind it; data storytelling communicates true findings from actual data using visuals and a clear narrative.

rw: The WHERE clause keeps only rows that satisfy a condition, such as price greater than 10, so it filters rows before results are returned.

ww.Joins tables on shared columns: Joining tables on shared columns is done by the JOIN clause, not by WHERE, which filters rows rather than combining tables.
ww.Groups rows by a column: Grouping rows by a column is the job of GROUP BY, whereas WHERE only filters individual rows by a condition.
ww.Sorts rows by a column value: Sorting rows by a column is done by ORDER BY, not WHERE, which filters rows instead of arranging them.

rw: GROUP BY collects rows sharing the same value in a column into groups, so aggregate functions such as COUNT or SUM can be computed per group.

ww.Filters rows that meet a given condition: Filtering rows that meet a condition is done by WHERE, whereas GROUP BY collects rows with shared values into groups for summarizing.
ww.Adds columns to a table that hold new va: Adding columns is done by altering a table or by computed expressions in SELECT, and GROUP BY does not create new columns of values.
ww.Deletes duplicates only from the table a: Removing duplicates is done with DISTINCT, and GROUP BY does group rows rather than remove them, so saying it groups no rows is false.

rw: A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables by matching values in a related column, such as a customer ID that appears in both tables.

ww.Deletes a table and all of the rows that: Deleting a table and its rows is done by DROP TABLE or DELETE, whereas a JOIN only reads and combines data without removing anything.
ww.Backs up a table to a second server for: Backing up a table to another server is a database administration task, whereas a JOIN is a query operation that merges rows from related tables.
ww.Sorts a table by a column and puts the r: Sorting by a column is done by ORDER BY, and a JOIN does not sort anything but combines rows from different tables using a related column.

rw: A primary key is a column, or set of columns, whose values uniquely identify each row, so no two rows share the same key value.

ww.A password that guards access to a datab: A password guards access, which is a security feature, whereas a primary key is a column that makes each row uniquely identifiable in the table.
ww.A chart that shows the rows of a table: A chart displays data visually, while a primary key is a structural database feature that gives each row a unique identity.
ww.A column that repeats values from row to: A primary key must have unique values in every row, so a column that repeats values cannot serve as one.

rw: A foreign key is a column holding values that match the primary key in another table, which links the tables and maintains referential integrity.

ww.A duplicate row that appears twice in th: A duplicate row is a data quality problem and not a key; a foreign key is a column that points to the primary key of another table.
ww.A key from another country used to open: A foreign key is a database term for linking tables and has nothing to do with countries or branches abroad, despite the word foreign.
ww.A password that protects a table from ou: Passwords protect access, whereas a foreign key is a column whose values match a primary key in another table, creating a link between the two.

rw: A pivot table reorganizes data and aggregates it, such as summing sales by region and month, so patterns can be seen quickly in a compact summary.

ww.A table of passwords that stores the sec: A table of passwords is a security risk and unrelated to analysis; a pivot table summarizes and regroups data by categories.
ww.A hardware table that holds computers an: A hardware table for tools and computers is furniture; a pivot table is a software feature in spreadsheets that summarizes and reorganizes data.
ww.A table that rotates a screen so that th: A pivot table does not rotate a screen; the name refers to turning rows and columns into summary views, so it is a data tool, not a display feature.

rw: VLOOKUP searches the first column of a range for a value and returns a value from another column in the same row, such as a price for a product ID.

ww.Draws charts from a range of cells and p: Drawing charts is done with chart tools, whereas VLOOKUP searches for a value in a table and returns related data from the same row.
ww.Deletes duplicates from a column and kee: Removing duplicates is a separate data tool; VLOOKUP does not delete anything and instead finds a matching value to return a related value from another column.
ww.Sorts data in a range from smallest to l: Sorting arranges data in a range in order, which is a different feature, while VLOOKUP searches for a key and returns a matching value from the row.

rw: ETL stands for extract, transform, load: data is pulled from sources, cleaned and reshaped, then loaded into a target such as a warehouse for analysis.

ww.Email, text, letter, the three common wa: Email, text and letter do not form ETL; the acronym stands for extract, transform, load, which is a data pipeline process, not a messaging method.
ww.Encrypt, test, launch, the three steps i: Encrypt, test and launch do not spell ETL, which is a data engineering process that extracts, transforms and loads data, not a software release routine.
ww.Edit, type, link, the three common steps: Edit, type and link describe document writing, while ETL means extract, transform, load, a standard process in data engineering for moving and preparing data.

rw: Data mining applies statistics and algorithms to large datasets to find patterns and relationships that are not obvious, such as which products are bought together.

ww.Printing data on paper so that managers: Printing data on paper is reporting, not mining; data mining analyzes large datasets to uncover hidden patterns and relationships automatically.
ww.Deleting data from a table once it has b: Deleting data after use is data cleanup or retention management, whereas data mining analyzes existing data to find useful patterns.
ww.Digging for minerals deep in the ground: Digging minerals is physical mining; data mining only borrows the name because analysts extract valuable patterns from large datasets, and nothing is excavated from the ground.

rw: A/B testing shows two versions to comparable groups and measures a result such as clicks or purchases to decide which version performs better.

ww.Grading students on tests and giving the: Grading students gives scores for learning, whereas A/B testing compares two versions of a product, page or ad to see which one performs better.
ww.Testing alphabets to see which letters a: A/B testing does not involve alphabets; the letters label two versions, A and B, and the test measures which version performs better with users.
ww.Testing only one version of something to: Testing only one version gives nothing to compare against; A/B testing needs two versions shown to similar groups so the results can be compared.

rw: Ad B got more clicks from a randomly split audience, so it likely performs better, but a significance test must check that the gap is not due to chance.

ww.Nothing can be learned from the clicks t: The clicks are real evidence from a randomized test, so claiming nothing can be learned is wrong; a significance test can tell whether the difference is likely real.
ww.Both are identical in their results, wha: The two ads got different click counts, so calling them identical ignores the data; whether the difference is real depends on statistical significance.
ww.Ad A is certainly better, since it was s: Ad A being certainly better contradicts the data, since Ad B received more clicks; also the audience was split randomly, so exposure to more people is not shown.

rw: Churn is the rate at which customers stop buying from or subscribing to a company over a given period, such as 5 percent leaving each month.

ww.A profit margin that shows earnings as a: A profit margin shows earnings as a share of sales, whereas churn measures how many customers leave over a period, so it is a loss rate.
ww.Making butter from cream by churning it: Making butter is the dairy meaning of churning, but in business analytics churn means customers leaving, not cream turning into butter.
ww.Customer growth over time as more people: Customer growth over time describes gains, but churn measures losses, meaning the share of customers who leave during a period.

rw: A time series is a sequence of data points recorded at successive points in time, such as daily sales or monthly temperature, so order matters.

ww.A database table that holds records in r: A table of rows and columns describes data layout in a database, whereas a time series is data recorded in order across successive points in time.
ww.A list of random numbers made by a compu: A list of random numbers has no time ordering, but a time series is defined by observations recorded at successive points in time.
ww.A set of categories used to group data i: A set of categories used to group data into bins describes a histogram setup, not a time series, which has observations ordered across time.

rw: Seasonality is a pattern that repeats at regular, predictable intervals, such as higher retail sales every December, within a time series.

ww.A one-time spike in the data that happen: A one-time spike is an outlier or event, whereas seasonality is a pattern that repeats at regular intervals, so it does not happen only once.
ww.A data error caused by a mistake in reco: A recording error is a data quality issue, whereas seasonality is a real repeating pattern in the values at regular intervals.
ww.A random change in the data that follows: Seasonality follows a regular repeating schedule, such as yearly or weekly, so describing it as random with no regular pattern is the opposite of true.

rw: A trend is the long-term upward or downward direction of a time series, such as steadily rising prices over many years.

ww.A random jump in the data at one point: A random jump at one point is noise or an outlier, whereas a trend is a sustained movement in one direction over a long period.
ww.A repeating cycle that returns every yea: A repeating cycle that returns every year is seasonality, while a trend is a long-term rise or fall that does not repeat on a schedule.
ww.A data error caused by a recording mista: A recording mistake is a data error, whereas a trend is a real long-term direction in the data, not an error.

rw: AGI is hypothetical AI that could learn and carry out any intellectual task a human can, instead of being limited to one narrow job.

ww.AI for one task such as sorting mail or: AI built for a single task, such as sorting mail or playing chess, is narrow AI, which is the opposite of general intelligence across many tasks.
ww.A type of calculator that adds and multi: A calculator adds and multiplies on request but does not learn or reason across tasks, so it has nothing to do with artificial general intelligence.
ww.A spreadsheet that holds numbers in rows: A spreadsheet stores numbers in rows and columns, but it does not learn or reason like a human, so it is not AGI.

rw: Robotics covers the design, building and use of machines that carry out tasks, often with AI to perceive and decide, as in factory arms.

ww.Trading stocks only, buying and selling: Trading stocks is finance, not robotics; robotics concerns designing and using physical machines that perform tasks, often guided by AI.
ww.Writing poems and verses for readers in: Writing poems is literature, not robotics; robotics is the field that designs machines, often with AI, to carry out physical tasks.
ww.Cooking recipes for meals in a home kitc: Cooking recipes belong to the culinary world; robotics is about designing and using machines that perform tasks, though a robot might be built to cook.

rw: A heuristic is a practical shortcut or rule of thumb that quickly finds a good-enough solution when a perfect one would be too slow.

ww.A database query that pulls a set of rec: A database query retrieves stored records and has nothing to do with problem solving by shortcuts, whereas a heuristic is a practical rule for finding good-enough answers.
ww.A random guess always, made with no thou: A heuristic is not a random guess; it is an informed rule of thumb that uses experience or logic to reach good answers faster.
ww.A proven exact formula that always gives: An exact formula guaranteeing the one correct answer is an algorithm; a heuristic trades guaranteed exactness for speed and gives a good-enough answer.

rw: A generative AI model produces new content, such as text, images or audio, learned from patterns in its training data.

ww.A model that prints reports and sends th: Printing reports is a basic output task, not generative AI; generative models create new content like text, images or audio from patterns they learned.
ww.A model that deletes files from a disk t: Deleting files frees space and is a system utility, not generative AI, which instead produces new content such as writing or images.
ww.A model that only sorts data into groups: A model that only sorts data into groups is a classifier or clustering model, whereas generative models can create new text, images or audio.

rw: A prompt is the input instruction, question or context you give a generative model, and it shapes the response the model produces.

ww.The model's output, which is the answer: The model's output is the response it returns, which is the opposite end of the process; the prompt is the input given to it.
ww.The model's weights, the numbers it has: Weights are the learned numbers inside the model, not what a user types; a prompt is the instruction or question given to the model.
ww.The training data that was used to teach: Training data is used earlier to teach the model, whereas a prompt is what a user supplies at use time to request an output.

rw: A hallucination occurs when a model states fabricated or incorrect information confidently, such as inventing a citation, so its output cannot be trusted without checking.

ww.A model update that changes the code and: A model update changing the code is a release, not a hallucination; a hallucination is when a model generates confident but false or made-up information.
ww.A correct answer that is supported by fa: A correct answer backed by facts and sources is the opposite of a hallucination, which is false or fabricated content presented with confidence.
ww.A security feature that blocks hackers f: A security feature blocking hackers is protection, not a hallucination, which describes a model producing confident but false or invented information.

rw: A chatbot citing a book that does not exist is a hallucination, since the model confidently generates fabricated information that sounds plausible but is false.

ww.Overfitting: Overfitting is when a model memorizes training data and fails on new data, which does not describe inventing a nonexistent source.
ww.Encryption: Encryption protects data by scrambling it and has no connection to a chatbot inventing a source that does not exist.
ww.Normalization: Normalization scales data to a common range and does not describe a chatbot inventing a fake source.

rw: Prompt engineering crafts and refines the inputs given to a model, such as clear instructions and examples, so it produces more useful and accurate outputs.

ww.Fixing code bugs by testing and rewritin: Fixing code bugs is debugging, whereas prompt engineering is the skill of designing inputs so an AI model produces useful results.
ww.Building hardware such as chips and serv: Building chips and servers is hardware engineering, whereas prompt engineering works only with the text instructions given to an existing AI model.
ww.Training from scratch on a huge set of d: Training from scratch on a huge dataset is model development, whereas prompt engineering works with an already trained model by improving the input it receives.

rw: A token is a chunk of text, such as a whole word or part of a word, which is the basic unit that a language model reads and generates.

ww.A password that a user types to log in t: A password used to log in is an authentication credential, whereas a token in an LLM is a piece of text that the model reads and writes.
ww.A database key that links a record in on: A database key links records between tables, which is a data concept, whereas an LLM token is a small chunk of text the model processes.
ww.A coin that is used to pay for access to: A coin used to pay for service is a currency token; in a language model, a token is instead a piece of text, not a payment unit.

rw: Fine-tuning continues training an already pre-trained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset so that it performs better on that particular task.

ww.Deleting a model once it is old and repl: Deleting an old model is retirement, not tuning; fine-tuning keeps the model and trains it further on specific data for a task.
ww.Tuning a musical instrument before a con: Tuning an instrument is a musical activity; in machine learning, fine-tuning means adjusting a pre-trained model with additional task-specific data, not music.
ww.Printing a model on paper so that people: Printing a model on paper does nothing to improve its performance; fine-tuning actually continues training the model on specific data for a task.

rw: A pre-trained model has already learned from large data, so it can be reused as is or adapted by fine-tuning, which saves time and cost.

ww.A deleted model that was removed from th: A deleted model has been removed, whereas a pre-trained model has finished training on large data and is available to reuse or adapt.
ww.A hardware chip that is built into a com: A hardware chip is a physical component, whereas a pre-trained model is software with learned parameters that has already been trained on large data.
ww.An untrained model that has not yet seen: An untrained model has not seen data, which is the opposite of pre-trained; a pre-trained model has already learned from large amounts of data.

rw: RAG retrieves relevant documents and gives them to a language model along with the question, so answers are grounded in real sources instead of memory alone.

ww.Compressing images to make files smaller: Compressing images shrinks file sizes and has no link to language models; RAG combines a model with retrieved documents to ground its answers.
ww.Encrypting model weights so that only ap: Encrypting model weights protects them from unapproved readers and is a security task, whereas RAG supplies retrieved documents to improve answers.
ww.Training from scratch on a very large da: Training from scratch builds a new model over a long time, whereas RAG leaves the model as it is and adds retrieved documents when it answers.

rw: An AI agent perceives its environment through inputs and takes actions to reach goals, such as a software system that completes tasks on a user's behalf.

ww.A human travel agent who books flights a: A human travel agent is a person, not software; an AI agent is a system that senses its surroundings and acts to reach goals.
ww.A spreadsheet that holds numbers in rows: A spreadsheet only stores and calculates numbers when told to, and it neither perceives nor acts toward goals, so it is not an AI agent.
ww.A hardware cable that links a computer t: A hardware cable only carries signals between devices; it neither perceives nor decides, so it cannot be an AI agent that takes actions toward goals.

rw: Multimodal AI can process more than one type of data, such as text, images and audio, and can combine them to understand or generate content.

ww.AI with one task, such as sorting mail o: AI with one task, such as sorting mail or playing chess, is narrow AI, while multimodal AI handles more than one type of data.
ww.AI with only text, so that it cannot han: An AI limited to text is unimodal; multimodal AI can handle several kinds of data such as images and sound as well as text.
ww.AI with several monitors, so that it can: Multimodal does not refer to several monitors; mode here means a type of data, such as text or images, not a number of screens.

rw: Regression predicts a continuous numerical value, such as house price or temperature, by learning the relationship between input features and a number.

ww.Predicting a category or class label: Predicting a category or class label is classification, whereas regression predicts a continuous number such as a price or temperature.
ww.Grouping similar items without any label: Grouping similar items without labels is clustering, an unsupervised task, whereas regression predicts a numerical value from labeled examples.
ww.Reducing features in a large data set: Reducing features in a large data set is dimensionality reduction, which differs from regression, whose aim is to predict a continuous number.

rw: Temperature in degrees is a continuous number, and predicting a continuous numerical value is regression, so this task is regression.

ww.Clustering: Clustering groups similar items without labels and does not predict a specific number such as a temperature in degrees.
ww.Reinforcement: Reinforcement learning trains an agent through rewards and actions, which does not fit a model that predicts a number such as temperature from data.
ww.Classification: Classification predicts discrete categories such as sunny or rainy, but a temperature in degrees is a continuous number, so this task is regression.

rw: Assigning each email to one of two known categories, spam or not spam, is classification, which predicts a discrete class label.

ww.File compression: File compression shrinks file sizes, which is not a machine learning task for labeling emails as spam or not spam.
ww.Regression: Regression predicts a continuous number, but spam or not spam is a category, not a number, so this is not regression.
ww.Clustering: Clustering groups items without predefined labels, but here the emails are put into two known categories, spam and not spam.

rw: A test set is data kept aside from training, so it gives an honest measure of how well the model performs on new examples.

ww.Data used to train the model on its firs: Data used to train the model is the training set, whereas a test set is held back and used only for evaluating the finished model.
ww.Data with errors only, which is removed: A test set is not made only of errors; it holds ordinary held-out examples that are used to check how well the model generalizes.
ww.Data about quizzes that are given to stu: Data about quizzes given to students has nothing to do with machine learning; a test set is held-out data that evaluates a model on new examples.

rw: A validation set is used during development to tune settings such as hyperparameters and choose between models, without touching the final test set.

ww.Data used for final scoring only, after: Final scoring after the build uses the test set, whereas a validation set is used during development to compare and tune the model.
ww.Data used for the first training only, b: First training uses the training set, whereas a validation set is a separate group of data used afterward to check progress and tune settings.
ww.Data about validation codes sent to user: Validation codes sent by email are unrelated to machine learning; a validation set is data used to tune model settings while the model is being developed.

rw: A 99% training score but only 62% on test data means the model memorized the training set and fails on new data, which is overfitting.

ww.Great fit: A great fit would perform well on both training and test data, but a drop from 99% to 62% shows the model fails on new data.
ww.Underfitting: Underfitting gives poor scores even on training data, but this model scores 99% on training data, so it is learning the training set well.
ww.Too little data: Too little data could contribute, but the main sign is a huge gap between training and test scores, which points to overfitting rather than data amount alone.

rw: More data, regularization and simpler models all help prevent a model from memorizing noise, so they reduce overfitting and improve results on new data.

ww.Using a more complex model only, and not: Using a more complex model only makes memorizing training noise easier, so it tends to increase overfitting instead of reducing it.
ww.Removing the test set from the data enti: Removing the test set would hide overfitting rather than cure it, because the test set is what reveals how well the model works on new data.
ww.Training longer on the same data to fit: Training longer on the same data lets the model fit noise more closely, which tends to worsen overfitting rather than reduce it.

rw: K-means is an unsupervised algorithm that groups data into k clusters by assigning each point to the nearest cluster center, with no labels needed.

ww.A chart that shows data as bars, lines o: A chart that shows data as bars, lines or slices is a visualization, while k-means is a clustering algorithm that groups data points.
ww.A supervised classifier that needs label: A supervised classifier needs labeled examples, but k-means works without labels, so it is unsupervised and not a classifier.
ww.A data cleaning step that removes duplic: Removing duplicates and fixing errors is data cleaning, whereas k-means is a clustering algorithm that sorts points into k groups by similarity.

rw: Logistic regression outputs a probability between 0 and 1 for a yes or no outcome, such as whether a customer will buy.

ww.Clustering data into groups of similar i: Clustering groups similar items, which is done by algorithms such as k-means, whereas logistic regression predicts the probability of a binary outcome.
ww.Storing data in a database on a large se: Storing data on a server is a database job, while logistic regression is a statistical model used to predict a probability of a binary outcome.
ww.Predicting continuous values such as pri: Predicting continuous values such as prices is the job of linear regression, whereas logistic regression predicts the probability of a binary outcome.

rw: Weights are adjustable numbers on connections between neurons that set how strongly one neuron influences the next, and training changes them to reduce error.

ww.Chart axes that show the scale of the va: Chart axes show the scale of plotted values, which is a visualization term, whereas weights are learned numbers inside a neural network.
ww.Data labels that name each point or bar: Data labels name points on a chart and are a plotting feature, whereas weights are learned numbers inside the network that scale signals between neurons.
ww.Physical weights used on a scale to meas: Physical weights measure mass on a scale, but in neural networks, weights are learned numbers on connections, with no physical mass involved.

rw: Backpropagation computes how much each weight contributed to the error by sending the error backward through the network, then adjusts the weights to reduce it.

ww.Storing results of each run in a file fo: Storing results of each run in a file is logging or saving, whereas backpropagation is the algorithm that sends error backward to update weights.
ww.Deleting layers from the network to make: Deleting layers makes a network smaller, which is called pruning, whereas backpropagation updates the weights using the error that is passed backward.
ww.Sending data forward only, from inputs t: Sending data forward only is the forward pass, but backpropagation does the reverse, passing errors backward to adjust the weights in training.

rw: Gradient descent repeatedly adjusts parameters in the direction that lowers the error, taking small steps until the error stops shrinking much.

ww.A type of chart that shows values as bar: A chart showing values as bars, lines or slices is a visualization, whereas gradient descent is an optimization method used in training models.
ww.A data cleaning step that removes duplic: Removing duplicate rows and fixing errors is data cleaning, whereas gradient descent is an optimization method that adjusts model parameters to reduce error.
ww.A way to climb hills by taking small ste: Gradient descent is not about hiking; the hill is only an image for the error surface, and the method steps downhill to reduce error, not to climb.

rw: The learning rate is a hyperparameter that sets how large each weight update step is, so a value too high overshoots and too low slows training.

ww.The accuracy of the model as the share o: The share of correct answers is accuracy, a performance metric, whereas the learning rate is a setting chosen before training.
ww.How fast a person learns, shown by lesso: How fast a person learns is a human trait, whereas in machine learning the learning rate is a hyperparameter for the model's update size.
ww.The number of layers in a neural network: The number of layers and their sizes describe the network's architecture, whereas the learning rate controls how big each update step is.

rw: An epoch is one complete pass of the learning algorithm through the entire training dataset, so training for 10 epochs means 10 passes.

ww.A data error that occurs during training: A data error during training would be a bug, whereas an epoch is a normal counting unit that measures one complete pass through the training data.
ww.A type of model used to make predictions: A type of model used for predictions would be an algorithm, whereas an epoch counts complete passes over the training data.
ww.A time of day when a model is trained: An epoch does not refer to a time of day; it counts how many times the model has seen the whole training set.

rw: CNNs use convolution layers that scan for local patterns like edges, which makes them excellent for processing images, as in photo classification and face detection.

ww.Stock price forecasts: Stock price forecasting is usually done by time series models, whereas CNNs are best known for working with images.
ww.Storing data files: Storing data files is a job for file systems or databases, not neural networks like CNNs, which are known for image processing.
ww.Sorting numbers: Sorting numbers is done by simple sorting algorithms, not CNNs, which are known for processing images by finding visual patterns.

rw: A transformer is a neural network architecture that uses attention to weigh relationships between tokens, and it underlies most modern language models.

ww.An electrical device that changes the vo: An electrical transformer changes voltage in power lines, but in AI the term names a neural network design, so the electrical device is a different thing.
ww.A database tool that stores tables of re: A database tool stores tables of records for search, whereas a transformer in AI is a neural network architecture built around attention.
ww.A robot toy that changes its shape from: A toy robot that changes shape is a product from a toy line, but in AI a transformer is a neural network architecture using attention.

rw: Accuracy is the number of correct predictions divided by the total number of predictions, so 90 correct out of 100 gives an accuracy of 0.9.

ww.The model's speed measured in seconds pe: Speed in seconds per run measures efficiency, not correctness; accuracy is the share of predictions that the model gets right.
ww.The share of errors that the model makes: The share of mistakes is the error rate, which is 1 minus accuracy, so it measures the opposite of what accuracy reports.
ww.The number of features in the data table: The number of features describes the size of the data table and is not a performance measure like accuracy, which counts correct predictions.

rw: Precision asks how many of the items predicted positive are truly positive, so it measures how reliable positive predictions are.

ww.Of the actual positives, the share the m: The share of actual positives that the model found is recall, not precision; precision looks at predicted positives instead of actual positives.
ww.The overall share of correct answers tha: The overall share of correct answers is accuracy, which counts both positives and negatives, whereas precision only looks at items predicted positive.
ww.The number of features in the data set u: The number of features describes the data set and is not a performance metric, whereas precision measures how many predicted positives are correct.

rw: Recall is true positives divided by all actual positives, so it shows what share of real positive cases the model correctly found.

ww.The overall share of correct answers tha: The overall share of correct answers is accuracy, whereas recall looks only at actual positives and asks how many the model found.
ww.The model's speed in seconds per run on: Speed in seconds per run measures how fast the model works, not whether it finds the actual positives, which is what recall measures.
ww.Of the predicted positives, the share th: The share of predicted positives labeled correctly is precision, which divides by predicted positives, whereas recall divides by actual positives.

rw: Recall measures the share of actual disease cases the model finds, so a high recall means few missed cases, which matters most for serious diseases.

ww.Run time: Run time measures speed and says nothing about whether serious cases are missed, so it does not guard against missing a disease.
ww.Model size: Model size tells how much memory the model needs, not whether it catches sick patients, so it does not address the risk of missed cases.
ww.Precision: Precision measures how many predicted positives are correct, so it guards against false alarms, but missing cases is a recall concern.

rw: Class imbalance means one class has far more examples than the others, which can lead a model to favor the majority class.

ww.Equal class sizes in every part of the d: Equal class sizes would be balance, not imbalance; class imbalance means the classes are not equal in size across the data.
ww.A missing label on one record in the dat: A missing label on one record is a data gap, not class imbalance, which concerns how unevenly examples are spread across classes.
ww.A cleaning step that removes duplicates: Removing duplicates is a cleaning step and has no link to class imbalance, which is about classes having very uneven numbers of examples.

rw: With 99% negatives, always guessing negative scores 99% while detecting no positives, so accuracy can mislead when classes are imbalanced; recall or precision would reveal the failure.

ww.The data is perfect and has no errors in: A model that always predicts negative learns nothing and misses every positive case, so 99% accuracy says nothing about perfect data or an absence of errors.
ww.Accuracy is always best, as a high score: Accuracy is not always best; here 99% accuracy hides a model that finds none of the positives, so a high score alone does not prove quality.
ww.The model is excellent and cannot be imp: A model that always predicts negative finds zero positive cases, so calling it excellent is wrong; its 99% only reflects how common negatives are.

rw: Anomaly detection finds unusual data points that differ from the norm, such as fraud in card transactions or faulty readings from a sensor.

ww.Sorting data into order from the smalles: Sorting data from smallest to largest is ordering, whereas anomaly detection finds unusual points that differ from the typical pattern.
ww.Cleaning duplicates from a table of reco: Cleaning duplicates from a table is data preparation, whereas anomaly detection identifies unusual points that differ from the norm.
ww.Finding the average of all of the values: Finding the average of all values is a summary statistic, whereas anomaly detection looks for the few points that differ strongly from that norm.

rw: MLOps covers practices for deploying, monitoring and maintaining machine learning models in production, combining machine learning with operations so models keep working reliably over time.

ww.A programming language used to write the: A programming language is used to write code, whereas MLOps is a set of practices for running models in production, not a language itself.
ww.A type of model that makes predictions f: A type of model that predicts from labeled data is supervised learning, whereas MLOps is about operating models, not creating predictions itself.
ww.A chart that shows data as bars, lines o: A chart showing bars, lines or slices is a visualization, whereas MLOps concerns deploying, monitoring and maintaining models in production.

rw: Model drift is the decline in a deployed model's performance as real-world data change from the data it was trained on, so retraining may be needed.

ww.A model moving files from one folder to: Moving files between folders is file management, whereas model drift describes a deployed model getting worse as real-world data changes.
ww.A model updating itself every night by d: A model that downloads new code each night would be an automated update, not drift, which is a decline in performance as data change.
ww.A model improving its results over time: Improving results with more users would be learning, but drift is the opposite, a decline in performance when real data move away from training data.

rw: Python is the most widely used language for data science and machine learning because of its simple syntax and rich libraries such as pandas and scikit-learn.

ww.HTML: HTML is a markup language that structures web pages, and it cannot perform data analysis or train machine learning models.
ww.Assembly: Assembly is a low-level language that is hard to write and read, so it is rarely used for data science or machine learning.
ww.CSS: CSS only styles how web pages look, so it is not used for data science or machine learning, which require a programming language.

rw: Pandas provides DataFrames, table-like structures that make it easy to clean, filter, group and analyze data in Python.

ww.Editing photos and images to fix colors: Editing photos is done in image editors, whereas pandas is a Python library for working with data tables.
ww.Playing music and songs from a library o: Playing music is a job for audio players, whereas pandas is a Python library for working with tabular data.
ww.Building websites and web pages with cod: Building websites uses web frameworks and HTML, whereas pandas handles data manipulation and analysis with DataFrames.

rw: NumPy provides fast arrays and math operations on them, so Python can handle large numerical data much more efficiently than plain lists.

ww.Drawing web pages with colors and fonts: Drawing web pages with colors and fonts is the job of HTML and CSS, while NumPy provides fast numerical computing in Python.
ww.Sending emails to clients and staff: Sending emails is the job of mail libraries and not NumPy, which is a library for fast numerical work with arrays.
ww.Editing video clips for films and posts: Editing video is done in video software, while NumPy supplies fast numerical array computing that data science tools build upon.

rw: Scikit-learn is a Python library that offers ready-made tools for classical machine learning, such as regression, classification, clustering and model evaluation.

ww.A database that stores records in tables: A database stores records in tables, but scikit-learn is a Python library of machine learning tools rather than a place for storing data.
ww.A text editor for writing plain notes an: A text editor is for writing notes, whereas scikit-learn is a Python library with tools for classical machine learning models.
ww.A web browser for viewing pages and site: A web browser views pages online, whereas scikit-learn is a Python library offering machine learning tools for data analysis.

rw: TensorFlow and PyTorch are frameworks that provide tools for building, training and running neural networks, including automatic gradient calculation and GPU support.

ww.Word processors used for writing letters: Word processors are used to write letters, whereas TensorFlow and PyTorch are frameworks for building and training neural networks.
ww.Spreadsheet programs used for sums, tabl: Spreadsheet programs handle sums and charts, whereas TensorFlow and PyTorch are frameworks for building and training neural networks.
ww.Web servers that deliver pages to browse: Web servers deliver pages to browsers, whereas TensorFlow and PyTorch are deep learning frameworks for neural networks.

rw: Matplotlib is a Python library for creating charts and visualizations, such as line plots, bar charts and scatter plots, from data.

ww.A web server that sends pages to browser: A web server sends pages to browsers, whereas Matplotlib is a Python library used to create charts and visualizations.
ww.A database that stores records in tables: A database stores records in tables, whereas Matplotlib is a Python library that draws charts and visualizations from data.
ww.A model that sorts images into groups fo: A model that sorts images into groups is a classifier, whereas Matplotlib is a plotting library that draws charts from data.

rw: GPUs have thousands of cores that do many calculations at the same time, which suits the matrix math in training and speeds it up.

ww.They store files on disks and keep them: Storing files on disks is the work of storage drives, not GPUs, which are built to carry out many calculations in parallel.
ww.They print documents for users who need: Printing documents is the work of printers, not GPUs, which are used in AI because they process many calculations in parallel.
ww.They connect to Wi-Fi networks so that d: Connecting to Wi-Fi is done by network adapters, not GPUs, which are used in AI because of their parallel processing power.

rw: Git records each change to code, lets you restore earlier versions, and allows many people to work together without overwriting each other's work.

ww.Cleaning data by removing errors and gap: Cleaning data by removing errors and gaps is data preparation, whereas version control such as Git tracks changes to code and helps teams collaborate.
ww.Training models on large sets of example: Training models on examples uses machine learning frameworks, whereas Git tracks changes to code and helps people work together.
ww.Making charts and graphs from the data: Making charts from data is done with plotting tools, whereas Git records changes to code and supports collaboration among team members.

rw: Tableau and Power BI let users build interactive visualizations and dashboards from data, which makes insights easy to explore and share.

ww.Writing code only, with no charts or oth: Writing code only is not their purpose, since both tools offer visual drag and drop interfaces for building charts and dashboards from data.
ww.Editing videos and adding music, titles: Editing videos is done in video software, whereas Tableau and Power BI are business intelligence tools for building dashboards and visualizations.
ww.Hosting websites on servers so that page: Hosting websites is done by web servers, whereas Tableau and Power BI are business intelligence tools for building dashboards and visualizations.

rw: A relational database stores data in tables with rows and columns, and relates the tables through keys, so queries can combine data from several tables.

ww.A folder of images stored on a computer: A folder of images is a collection of files, whereas a relational database stores data in tables that are linked by keys.
ww.A text file that holds plain notes and w: A text file with plain notes has no tables or relations, so it is not a relational database, which stores data in linked tables.
ww.A database of family members and birthda: Relational refers to relationships between data tables made through keys, not family relatives, so a database of family members is not what the term means.

rw: A NoSQL database stores data in flexible formats such as documents, key-value pairs or graphs, rather than only in the fixed rows and columns of traditional tables.

ww.A spreadsheet only, with no tables, keys: A spreadsheet is a different tool, whereas a NoSQL database stores data in flexible formats and does include records, although not necessarily in tables.
ww.A database with no data in it at all, so: A NoSQL database holds data, which can be documents, key-value pairs or graphs, so saying it has no data at all is wrong.
ww.A paper record kept in a filing cabinet: A paper record in a filing cabinet is not a digital database at all, whereas NoSQL is a database type that stores data in flexible formats.
